name: The Cold Lands
overview: The Cold Lands are the largest and least known country of Aoaz, a white land of snow plain, three great ranges and a winter so long that the clans count the year in two halves, the Long Dark and the Long Light. Men have herded reindeer and hunted seal here since before Aen, and the giants of the north-west heights and the yeti of the shelf and the high snows are older still in the clans' tales. Aenor's First Age ships charted the coast and left trading posts behind them, but no southern crown ever ruled the interior, and when Aenor fell to the Necromancer the north was too far and too cold to be worth his taking. Its own history turns on bread rather than ore: the chief who opened his stores in the Hunger Winters founded the custom from which the Winter Crown of Coldor grew, and in 4A 850 that crown brought the frozen interior under one rule, while the warlords of Melkgard behind their black forts refused it and have refused it ever since. In 4A 1748 Coldor and Horidor keep the Northern Accord, Melkgard keeps its forts manned, the Free Steadings of Fearno answer to neither, goblins tend the warm springs of the southern valleys, and in the valley of Mp'E an ordinary town lives below a silent castle whose lord nobody visits. Years in the data are one continuous count from the victory of Aen on the proposed lengths of the ages (First Age 1,675 years, Second Age 2,133, Third Age 1,260): 1A 1 is year 1, 2A 1 is 1,676, 3A 1 is 3,809 and 4A 1 is 5,069, so that the campaign year 4A 1748 is 6,816; every entry also carries its date in the Age-and-year form, which is the form the prose uses.

ages.name: The Age of the Sunfields
ages.summary: Long before Aen, when the ice lay far to the north, the first men of the north-west held the Fandan meadows, the interior that is now the Frozen Lands and the coast below the Icy Mountains: the Sunfields, with great timber halls, bronze, horse-herds and the first sea-craft of Aoaz. The winters lengthened over many lifetimes, the halls emptied and the realm broke into clans who went three ways: south over the neck, west by sea to the arcs, and into the Long Dark.

ages.name: The Charts and the Posts
ages.summary: Aenoran ships reached the Cold Lands early in the First Age, named the coast Coldor, the ice-land, on their charts and set trading posts at Alorio and the Fandan mouth, where they bought furs, amber and walrus ivory from clans who had never heard of a king. Around 1A 400 Aenoran surveyors with clan guides drew the first road over the Neridor Gap, the line that later became the Neck Road. The clans who showed Aenor's surveyors the Neck Road had never heard of a king, because their kings had been gone for a thousand years.

ages.name: The Free Harbours
ages.summary: As Aenor weakened under its bad kings the northern posts passed to clan chiefs, and Alorio and the Fandan mouth became free harbours that paid nothing to Parim. The Cold Lands sent no banners to Dardan, and the clans remember the war of the south only as the southern burning, a glow on the traders' faces when they came north again.

ages.name: The Hunger Winters and the Frost-Hall
ages.summary: The plagues of the Age of Long Grief came north by ship, and three bitter winters in one generation broke the coastal clans until the Fandan chief Kolar opened his stores to every clan that came to his fire. The custom of bread that his line kept grew into the first Frost-Hall at Fandanar in 2A 600, and around 2A 1000 goblin warrens crossed the Coldor Channel's winter ice and settled the warm-spring valleys of the southern mountains.

ages.name: The Pacts and the Black Forts
ages.summary: The clans made their old pacts with the elder peoples of the snow, a hunting truce with the shelf yeti at Fentene and a toll-peace with the ice giants of the heights, and the snowline fair grew from the first. In the same centuries warlords fortified the Ormolak valley against sea-raiders from the north coast and cut the Black Gallery into the rock below Minnolomak, the beginning of the march that became Melkgard.

ages.name: The Far Refuge
ages.summary: The Necromancer's Order never reached the Cold Lands. Aenoran families fled north by sea in small numbers, the western trade replaced the southern at Alorio, and the one time his servants came, to buy the dead of a starving clan in 3A 702, the Fandan chiefs burned their ship in Fandhavn harbour and made the burning of the dead the first law of the Winter Hearth.

ages.name: The Winter Crown
ages.summary: From 4A 850 the Winter Crown of Coldor rules the frozen interior and the western ports and leads the Northern Accord with Horidor, while Melkgard refuses it and the Free Steadings of Fearno stand apart from both. The age is one of raids across the Fandan rather than declared wars, of western grain bought over the Neck Road and of crowns that buy the clans' loyalty one hard winter at a time.

countries.name: Coldor

founding.story: The kings of the Fandan valley had kept the Frost-Hall's bread for six centuries before Queen Ilvra of the Vording line called the clan-fire keepers to Fandanar in 4A 850 and was crowned with a circlet of white iron as the first Winter Queen. Every clan of the frozen interior that had eaten from the crown granaries in a hard winter swore to her, and at the Neridor Gap Horidor's chiefs swore the Northern Accord beside them; only the warlords of the Ormolak valley sent back her envoys unfed.

roots.story: When the winters of the Sunfields lengthened and the ice came south over the Fandan meadows, the clans that would not leave the north gathered at the last of the old king's halls, and when that hall too was given to the snow its fire-keepers did not let the fire die. They carried a coal of the hall's hearth in an aurochs horn lined with clay and bound with bronze, feeding it through the first Long Dark that men of the north ever lived through, and from that coal every clan that stayed relit its fire. Out of that winter came the hearth-law that still rules the Cold Lands: no feud may be carried past a shared fire, a house that lets its fire die in the Long Dark relights it only from the clan fire, and whoever keeps the fire must feed whoever reaches it. The horn passed from keeper to keeper among the Fandan clans for longer than any song can count; it was at the horn's fire that Kolar fed every clan in the Hunger Winters, and around it that the first Frost-Hall was raised in 2A 600. The Winter Crown is therefore a crown of keepers rather than conquerors: its queens are crowned with a hand on the horn, its fire-keepers teach that the land was punished and the fire is what was spared, and its whole authority in 4A 1748 still rests on the promise the old keepers made, that whoever reaches the fire will eat.

sign.device: The Ember-Horn: a curved horn bound with bronze bands, mouth upward, with a single red coal glowing at its mouth, gold and red on a deep night-blue field, with a white hem of square hearth-stones.
sign.origin: The Ember-Horn is the clay-lined aurochs horn in which the last fire-keepers of the Sunfields carried a coal of the old king's hearth into the first Long Dark. It hangs in the Frost-Hall above the fire that the keepers say has never gone out, and Queen Ilvra I was crowned with her hand on it in 4A 850. The clans had sewn the horn on their moot-cloths long before there was a crown, as the mark of a fire that feeds all comers, and when the Winter Crown raised its first banner it took the clans' mark instead of inventing one, so that no clan could say the crown had come from outside the hearth.
sign.meaning: Bread and fire for every clan that comes to the hearth in the Long Dark, and the hearth-law over every feud; to an enemy it says that the crown's strength is a store and a fire, and that the clans who have eaten from it remember.

dynasties.name: The Kolaring, bread-chiefs of the Fandan
dynasties.notable: Descended from Kolar, the chief who opened his stores to every clan in the Hunger Winters; they raised the first Frost-Hall in 2A 600 and ruled the valley as chiefs until the crown was made.

dynasties.name: House Vording, the Winter Crown
dynasties.notable: Founded by Queen Ilvra I, a daughter of the Kolaring through her mother; the crown passes to the eldest child of either sex, and Queen Vaestia, who reigns in 4A 1748, is the eleventh ruler of the line.

events.name: The Carrying of the Coal
events.summary: As the last of the old king's halls was given to the snow, its fire-keepers carried a coal of the hearth into the first Long Dark in a clay-lined horn, and every clan that stayed in the north relit its fire from it.

events.name: The Hearth of the Last Hall
events.summary: The fire-keepers relight every house-fire of the clan from the clan fire in the Long Dark, a custom they say is older than any crown and was the custom of the last hall of the Sunfields.

events.name: The Hunger Winters
events.summary: Three bitter winters in one generation broke the coastal clans after plague came north by ship, and the Fandan chief Kolar fed every clan that reached his fire, the act from which the crown later took its right to the granaries.

events.name: The March of Bones
events.summary: Servants of the Necromancer's Order bought the dead of a starving coast clan; the Fandan chiefs rode to Fandhavn, burned the buyers' ship at its moorings and made the burning of the dead the law of every Coldic hearth.

events.name: The Winter Crown
events.summary: Queen Ilvra I was crowned at Fandanar and the Northern Accord was sworn with Horidor at the Neridor Gap; Melkgard refused the crown and the rivalry of the two halves of the Ormolak country began.

events.name: The Forty Winters' Quarrel
events.summary: For forty winters Fandanar and Minnolomak raided each other across the frozen Fandan without ever declaring war, and both sides built the March Forts on the river banks that still stand manned.

events.name: The Neck Road Compact
events.summary: Coldor, Horidor and Worlond agreed with Gunwyn's king to keep the Neck Road open from the thaw to the first snows, western grain and cattle going north for Coldic iron, furs and timber; the crown granaries at Fandanar and Alorio have been filled by it ever since.

events.name: The White Year
events.summary: The worst winter in living memory closed the Neck Road for two summers; Coldor opened its granaries to Pertolor, Omar and Xison as well as its own clans, and the crown's lean among the moors has never been higher.

rivalries.nature: The Cold Rivalry since 4A 850: the warlords refused the Winter Crown and the March Forts face each other across the Fandan.
The Free Steadings refused the crown in 4A 1304; Fandanar courts their lords with grain and is courteously refused.

countries.capitalReason: Fandanar stands where the Neck Road leaves the Fandan for the high country, in the one valley whose sedge meadows feed horses through the Long Light; the first Frost-Hall was raised here around a fire carried from the eastern Fandan clans, and the crown granaries stand beside it.
countries.today: Queen Vaestia rules some eight hundred thousand people from the Frost-Hall, the strongest crown of the north and the least warlike, whose real power is the bread in its granaries and the grain bought each summer over the Neck Road. The Accord with Horidor holds, the clans still remember the White Year, the March Forts are manned against Melkgard, and the Houses of the First Light keep a small hospital and grain-roll at Alorio for the port.

divergence.what: Coldor's wardens hear of the stranger found in the far north-west ice and summon him to Fandanar instead of letting the clans nurse him.
divergence.consequence: The road south is delayed by about a month and the stranger owes the Winter Crown a debt of hospitality; the clans who found him resent the crown's hand.

divergence.what: The queen settles the Cold Rivalry by the Iron Hand, crossing the Fandan in force while Melkgard's oath-companies are scattered.
divergence.consequence: Melkgard can be made to kneel, but the Free Steadings and the border clans fear the crown more than they love its bread, and Fearno looks for friends elsewhere.

divergence.what: Coldor sends its White Companies south with timber and ships for the coalition of the living instead of standing apart in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The Cold Lands enter the War of the Last Crowns for the first time in their history, and the crown's granaries empty faster than the Neck Road can refill them.

divergence.what: The Ember-Horn is carried out of the Frost-Hall by a raid or a conqueror, or its coal is let die.
divergence.consequence: The clans no longer count the crown's hearth-right as sacred and every clan's lean toward Fandanar falls; whoever holds the horn can claim to keep the hearth-law, and the fire-keepers must relight the Frost-Hall's fire from a clan fire, which no queen has ever had to ask.

countries.name: Melkgard

founding.story: Sea-raiders from the north coast had burned the Ormolak valley for a generation when a chief named Zorak brought the valley's men under one oath in 2A 1780, set them to cut the Black Gallery into the cliff below Minnolomak and built the first of the black-stone forts that give the march its name, melk for black and gard for the stronghold. He took no crown and left none: the march has been held ever since by the best sworn man of the oath-companies, chosen over the warlord's pyre.

roots.story: The Ormolak valley was never a land of the hearth-keepers. The clans who came up its sheltered floor after the Sunfields fell were hunters and bog-smiths, and for longer than the songs can count they were raided from the Frozen Ocean coast by sea-wolves whose home no southern chart has fixed. The march's own tale says that in 2A 1779 Zorak, a bog-smith's son, went down into the cliff below Minnolomak where the north wind howls through the rock and bargained there with the storm that had sunk more raiders than any warrior had killed. What answered him the Storm Court calls the Black Wind; the fire-keepers of Fandanar say it was one of the corrupted servants who fled an Old God and came to Aoaz, a devil by its true name, and the march will hear neither word spoken aloud. Zorak forged a gauntlet of black iron from the keel-bolts of the first raider ship the wind broke, swore his men into it hand by hand, and set them to cut the Black Gallery, where the wind's token still hangs. From that bargain come the laws of the march: no warlord wears a crown, because Zorak promised the wind that no man of the valley would rule by birth; every oath is sworn with the hand inside the gauntlet; a token is kept for every wind that sinks an enemy; and the oath-companies would rather go hungry than eat bread they did not take or earn. The Iron Crown that hangs unworn in the Black Gallery is the crown Zorak refused, and Melkgard's refusal of the Winter Crown in 4A 850 was, to the march, only the same refusal said again.

sign.device: The Sworn Gauntlet: a black iron gauntlet raised with its fist closed, on a storm-grey field, with a black hem of jagged teeth.
sign.origin: Zorak forged the gauntlet from the keel-bolts of the first raider ship that the Black Wind drove onto the rocks of the Gulf of Minnolomak, and every oath-man of the first companies swore by putting his hand inside it while Zorak closed his own hand over the iron. The gauntlet was burned with him on his pyre and taken out of the ashes whole, which the march counts as the wind's answer, and since then each new warlord is chosen over his predecessor's pyre with the gauntlet on his hand and never a crown on his head. The oath-companies painted the closed fist on their shields before the march had any banner, and the black-stone forts fly it on grey.
sign.meaning: A realm held by the sworn hand and never by birth or crown: to its own men it promises that an oath binds the warlord as much as the sworn, and to Fandanar it says that the march will kneel to no fire it did not light.

dynasties.name: The oath-heirs of the Black Gallery
dynasties.notable: No family holds Melkgard; each warlord is chosen by the oath-companies from among the men sworn to his predecessor. Warlord Grinek, who sent Queen Ilvra's envoys home unfed in 4A 850, is the most honoured of them, and Warlord Ezhan Isenmar holds the march in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Bargain in the Cliff
events.summary: Zorak went down into the windy cliff below Minnolomak and came back with the token of the Black Wind; that winter a raider fleet broke on the rocks of the gulf, and he forged the Sworn Gauntlet from the keel-bolts of its first ship.

events.name: The Cutting of the Black Gallery
events.summary: Zorak's oath-men cut the long gallery into the cliff below Minnolomak, where the Storm Court keeps a token of every wind that has sunk a raider's ship, and raised the first black forts of the march.

events.name: The Raiders Broken
events.summary: The last great fleet of north-coast raiders broke on the forts of the Gulf of Minnolomak, and its survivors settled as sealers on the coast beyond, where their grandchildren became the folk of Portogalor.

events.name: The Refusal
events.summary: Warlord Grinek refused the Winter Crown when Coldor united the interior, and the march has kept that refusal as its founding pride.

events.name: The Forty Winters' Quarrel
events.summary: Forty winters of raids across the frozen Fandan, in which Melkgard took cattle and Coldor took hostages, ended in a cold peace and the March Forts on both banks.

events.name: The Bid for Guerlon
events.summary: Melkgard offered Orewele's mining clan protection in return for half its iron; the clan took Coldor's grain instead, and the warlords have bid for the Orewell mines in every generation since.

events.name: The Gifts of the White Year
events.summary: While Coldor opened its granaries, Melkgard sent salt meat and iron tools to Omar and the border moor, so that the clan nearest its forts owed it at the next moot.

rivalries.nature: The Cold Rivalry: the march has refused the Winter Crown since 4A 850 and measures its pride by never asking for the Accord.
The border clan Melkgard presses hardest, with gifts in hard winters and oath-demands in good ones.

countries.capitalReason: Minnolomak stands at the mouth of the main Ormolak pass on the Gulf of Minnolomak, where the valley's bog-ore and the rock-ore of the mountains meet a harbour; whoever holds it holds the only road between the north coast and the sheltered valley.
countries.today: Some three hundred thousand people live under Warlord Ezhan Isenmar and his oath-companies, in a march of forges and black forts whose men would rather go hungry than eat the queen's bread. The March Forts are manned, gifts flow to the border clans, the Storm Court's captains keep their tokens in the Black Gallery, and the warlord still bids for the Orewell iron.

divergence.what: A warlord chosen after a bad winter swears to the Northern Accord and takes a seat at the Frost Moot.
divergence.consequence: The Cold Rivalry ends without a war, Coldor's reach covers the whole interior and the oath-companies who refused the new warlord go south as sellswords.

divergence.what: The warlord sells passage through the Ormolak Pass to a southern temple party seeking the valley of Mp'E.
divergence.consequence: The party reaches the silent castle sooner and better guided; Coldor's watch-fires never see it pass, and the valley folk do not forgive the march.

divergence.what: Melkgard seizes the Orewell mines while Coldor is busy elsewhere.
divergence.consequence: The march gains the iron of the far north and the defiance to match it, and the western dwarves' factors deal with the warlord instead of the clan.

divergence.what: The Sworn Gauntlet is taken in a war on the march or lost with a warlord who dies far from his pyre.
divergence.consequence: The oath-companies hold their oaths void and the march breaks into its separate forts until a new warlord is chosen over an empty pyre; a crown that holds the gauntlet can offer it back for an oath, and the Storm Court's captains say the Black Wind will choose for itself.

countries.name: Horidor

founding.story: The clans of the lower Fandan had guided Aenor's surveyors over the Neridor Gap in the First Age and kept the cairns that marked the road after the southerners left. In 2A 340 their chiefs met at the drawn town below the Gap and swore to keep the cairn road open for every traveller who paid the cairn-due, and the cairn moot of Ollondo, the oldest standing moot of the Cold Lands, has met there every Long Light since.

roots.story: Horidor's clans say that the Neck Road was walked before it was cut. When the Sunfields' fields failed, a great part of its people went south over the neck toward the West Lands, and the road-wardens of the old king raised cairns along the Neridor Gap so that those who followed in the whiteout would not lose the way. The wardens' last order, as the clans tell it, was to keep the cairns standing until the walkers came home; nobody came home, and the wardens' children kept the cairns anyway, adding a stone each time they passed and setting a guide-pole bound with a red rag on the high cairns so that the road showed through the snow. The custom became law: a traveller who adds no stone pays the cairn-due instead, no clan may pull down a cairn even in war, and the moot of Ollondo exists to keep the road and not to rule the people beside it. When Aenor's surveyors came in 1A 400 the clans who guided them had never heard of a king, but they knew every cairn by name, and they keep the cairn-names still as their history: the high cairns are named for the wardens and the low ones for the travellers who died between them. In 4A 1748 Horidor counts its strength in passable miles rather than in men, greets the Gunwyn clans of the West Lands as the walkers who never came back, and knows that whoever closes the Gap closes the north.

sign.device: The Guide-Pole: a grey stepped cairn with a tall pole rising from its top, a red rag streaming from the pole, on a dark green field, with a white hem.
sign.origin: The red-ragged guide-pole is the mark the old road-wardens set on the high cairns of the Neridor Gap so that walkers could see the road through a whiteout, and every Horidor chief still sets one with his own hands on the highest cairn when he is chosen. The moot's first banner, raised at Ollondo in 2A 340, was a red rag tied to a pole and carried up the Gap ahead of the chiefs who swore to keep the road; it was sewn onto green cloth with the cairn beneath it when Chief Bransdok Azling carried it to the Gap to swear the Northern Accord in 4A 850.
sign.meaning: The road kept open for every traveller who pays the cairn-due and a way home for the walkers who never returned; to an enemy it says that the Gap is held by people who know every stone of it.

dynasties.name: The Azling cairn-chiefs
dynasties.notable: The moot chooses its chief from the Azling hearth-line more often than any other; Chief Bransdok Azling swore the Northern Accord at the Gap beside Queen Ilvra in 4A 850.

events.name: The Neck Road
events.summary: The road over the Neridor Gap is cut by the people of the Sunfields, and their descendants walk it south long after the halls behind them empty.

events.name: The Wardens' Cairns
events.summary: The road-wardens of the Sunfields raised cairns and red-ragged guide-poles along the Neridor Gap for the clans walking south, and their children kept the cairns standing after the walkers were gone.

events.name: The Charting of the Neck
events.summary: Horidor's forebears guided Aenoran surveyors over the Neridor Gap and helped them draw the first road from the Fandan to the West Lands, and they kept its cairns when the surveyors went home.

events.name: The Northern Accord
events.summary: Chief Bransdok swore mutual defence with the new Winter Crown at the Neridor Gap, and Horidor's chiefs have sat at the Frost Moot of Fandanar ever since.

events.name: The Neck Road Compact
events.summary: Horidor took the keeping of the cairn road and its stages over the Gap under the compact with Gunwyn, and the cairn-due became the moot's main income.

events.name: The Year of the Closed Gap
events.summary: An avalanche buried the high cairn road for a whole Long Light; Horidor's clans cut a new way around the slide by hand, and the western traders who waited at Tarvak still tell of it.

rivalries.nature: Horidor stands with Coldor in the Accord, and Melkgard's raiders have twice burned the lower Fandan steadings.

countries.capitalReason: Ollondo sits on the valley road just below the Neridor Gap, where travellers wait for the weather before the crossing and pay the cairn-due; the moot meets where the road is, because the road is what the moot exists to keep.
countries.today: About two hundred and twenty thousand people live along the lower Fandan and in the Neridor Mountains under the cairn moot. Horidor keeps the Accord faithfully, collects its dues from every western cart and remembers the White Year, when Coldor's bread came up the valley before the snow did.

divergence.what: The cairn moot closes the Gap to western travellers after a quarrel over dues.
divergence.consequence: The Neck Road shuts for a season, Coldor's granaries run low and any stranger coming south from the far north-west must wait in the Worlond Forest for the moot to relent.

divergence.what: A cairn-chief bought with Melkgard's gifts takes Horidor out of the Northern Accord.
divergence.consequence: Coldor loses the Gap, the Accord becomes a crown with no league, and the Neck Road becomes the price of every quarrel in the north.

divergence.what: A crown at war with Horidor pulls down the high cairns of the Neridor Gap.
divergence.consequence: The Neck Road can be crossed only with Horidor's guides, every clan of the north counts the act a crime against the oldest law of the road, and the offender's standing at every winter moot falls for a generation.

countries.name: Fearno

founding.story: The steading lords of the eastern moors had grazed the Naepu country since the Second Age without any lord above them, and when Fandanar and Minnolomak both sent envoys in 4A 1304 to ask their oath, they met in the hall at Azenoalion and agreed to refuse both. They named themselves the Free Steadings, chose a first lord to speak for them for seven winters, and swore that no steading would go hungry while another had stores.

roots.story: The steading lords of Fearno tell the end of the Sunfields differently from the fire-keepers of Fandanar. In their telling, when the fields failed the last king of the old hall called every clan to bring its herds to him so that the hall might live, and the moor clans of the Naepu, who saw that the herds would be eaten and the hall would empty all the same, bound their spears together on the river ice and refused him. The king's hall died that winter, the moor clans lived, and from that refusal the moor folk took the conviction that a crown eats first and feeds last. Their law came out of it: no lord above the lords, a first lord chosen only to speak and only for a term, every steading's stores open to a hungry neighbour, and a spear laid in the bundle by each lord at the moot to show that he is bound to the others and to nobody else. The Naepu clans kept the Spear-Binding through the Second Age while they learned to sow moor oats in the river bends, and when Fandanar and Minnolomak both sent for their oath in 4A 1304 the steading lords did at Azenoalion what their forebears had done on the river. In 4A 1748 the hall still argues for a month before it agrees, because agreement must be every lord's, and the Free Steadings are the one people of the north who would refuse a crown of the Sunfields even if it were offered to them as their own.

sign.device: The Bound Spears: seven upright spears bound together at the middle by a red cord, white on a dark moss-green field, with a brown hem of hide stitching.
sign.origin: Each steading lord brings his own spear to the hall at Azenoalion and lays it in the bundle when the moot opens; the red cord is tied round the bundle by the eldest lord present and cut by the first lord when the moot closes. The clans say the first bundle was tied on the Naepu ice when their forebears refused the last king of the old hall, and the banner of seven spears was first sewn for the Free Steadings in 4A 1304, one spear for each steading that swore the refusal; the banners of the Melkgard raiders lost on the open snow in 4A 1112 hang beneath it in the hall.
sign.meaning: Many lords bound to one another and to no crown: a promise that no steading goes hungry while another has stores, and a warning to Fandanar and Minnolomak alike that the bundle does not break one spear at a time.

dynasties.name: The first lords of the hall
dynasties.notable: A first lord is chosen for seven winters from among the steading lords; the Azening steading of the upper Naepu has given the hall more first lords than any other.

events.name: The Refusal on the River
events.summary: When the last king of the old hall called the clans to bring him their herds, the moor clans of the Naepu bound their spears together on the river ice and refused, and they lived while the hall died.

events.name: The Settling of the Naepu
events.summary: Reindeer clans settled the moors along the Naepu and learned to sow moor oats in its few sheltered bends, the beginning of the steadings.

events.name: The Naepu Raid
events.summary: Oath-companies of Melkgard rode across the frozen interior to burn Azenoalion and were lost in a whiteout on the open snow; the steadings buried the men they found in spring, and the hall keeps their banners.

events.name: The Free Steadings
events.summary: The steading lords refused both crowns at once and founded the hall of many lords at Azenoalion.

events.name: The Cold Tarn Fishing Feud
events.summary: Fearno and Austklev quarrelled over the char of the Cold Tarn until the Frost Moot of Fandanar arbitrated a sharing of the shores, one of the few times the steadings accepted the crown's judgement.

rivalries.nature: Fearno refuses the Winter Crown and its bread both, politely.
The Cold Tarn shores, divided by arbitration in 4A 1560 and quarrelled over every Long Light since.

countries.capitalReason: Azenoalion stands on the Naepu where the moor roads meet the river ice, a hall-town big enough to seat every steading lord and central enough that none of them rides further than the others.
countries.today: Some two hundred and fifty thousand herders live in the largest free realm of the north, a third pole between Fandanar and Minnolomak whose hall argues for a month before it agrees on anything. The present first lord leans neither way and means to keep it so.

divergence.what: The hall votes to join the Northern Accord after Coldor feeds the steadings in a bitter winter.
divergence.consequence: Coldor's Accord covers the whole east, and Melkgard stands alone against a united interior.

divergence.what: The first lord makes a pact with Melkgard against the crown's reach.
divergence.consequence: Coldor faces enemies on two sides of the snow, and the Cold Rivalry becomes a war the Accord might lose.

divergence.what: A first lord refuses to cut the cord when his seven winters end and keeps the bundle in his own steading.
divergence.consequence: The hall splits between the lords who call him a king and those who wait for him to yield; Fandanar and Minnolomak both offer to back him, and whichever does is hated by the steadings for a lifetime.

countries.name: Austklev

founding.story: Whaling crews from the eastern cliffs, the aust-klev of the Coldic name, had gathered at the sheltered harbour of Vaestia for generations before Jarl Kolim Ezhair built a hall there in 4A 612 and took a tithe of every whale brought ashore in return for keeping the harbour boom and the forest timber. The jarls have kept the hall and the tithe since, and the east coast takes its law from the harbour rather than from any crown.

roots.story: The east coast was not peopled from the Sunfields' meadows but from the sea. The jarls' tale is that a crew of seal-hunters, driven north-east by a gale out of the Siroler ice in a year no one counts, lost every landmark and followed a white spear-whale that surfaced ahead of them each morning until it led them through the pack into the sheltered water below the eastern cliffs, where it beached and died. The crew ate of it, built their first hall from its ribs and swore over its tusk never to hunt a white whale, to give the sea back the first catch of every season, and to land every whale at one harbour so that no crew could starve while another feasted. That oath is the root of the whale-tithe that Jarl Kolim Ezhair claimed when he built the harbour hall and its boom at Vaestia in 4A 612, and of the custom that a jarl must have captained a whaling crew, because the jarl is the one who has followed the whale. The Tusk of Vaestia still stands beside the jarl's seat, and every crew touches it before the first voyage of the Long Light. The east coast takes its law from that harbour rather than from any crown because, as the whalers say, the whale chose the harbour and no queen did, and in 4A 1748 the jarl still answers every envoy from Fandanar by pointing at the tusk.

sign.device: The Tusk of Vaestia: one long spiral whale-tusk standing upright, white on a deep sea-red field, with a black hem of curling waves.
sign.origin: The device is the tusk of the white spear-whale that led the first crew through the Siroler pack and beached itself below the cliffs, which the Ezhair jarls keep upright beside their seat in the harbour hall. Crews cut its shape into their prows long before the jarldom, and when Jarl Kolim Ezhair hung the harbour boom in 4A 612 he flew the tusk on red sailcloth from the winch-post, the red standing for the first catch of the season given back to the sea; it has flown there every Long Light since.
sign.meaning: The whale-oath: the first catch to the sea, every whale to one harbour and no white whale hunted; it promises a jarl who has followed the whale and tells the crowns that the east coast answers to its harbour.

dynasties.name: The Ezhair jarls of Vaestia
dynasties.notable: A coast family of whalers who keep the harbour hall; the jarldom passes to the son or daughter who has captained a whaling crew.

events.name: The Whale's Harbour
events.summary: A storm-driven crew of seal-hunters followed a white spear-whale through the Siroler pack to the sheltered water below the eastern cliffs, where it beached; they built a hall of its ribs and swore the whale-oath over its tusk.

events.name: The Hall at Vaestia
events.summary: Jarl Kolim Ezhair built the harbour hall and its boom and claimed the whale-tithe, founding the jarldom.

events.name: The Cold Tarn Fishing Feud
events.summary: Austklev's fishers and Fearno's steadings fought over the char of the Cold Tarn until the Frost Moot divided its shores.

events.name: The Ice-Lock
events.summary: An early freeze locked half the whaling fleet in the Siroler ice for a winter; the crews lived on their catch and walked home over the ice in spring, and the jarl since keeps a winter store at the harbour.

countries.capitalReason: Vaestia is the one deep, sheltered harbour of the east coast where the forest comes down to the sea, so that the whalers can build their ships and land their catch in the same place.
countries.today: About a hundred thousand people live by whaling, sealing and timber along the east coast facing the Siroler Seas. The jarl sells whale-fat and spear-whale tusk south and west, keeps out of the Cold Rivalry and watches the ice.

divergence.what: The jarl hires out his whaling fleet as transports for whichever crown pays in the last war.
divergence.consequence: A small but hardy northern fleet joins the war at sea, and the east coast's lamps go dim for want of whale-fat at home.

divergence.what: Austklev joins the Northern Accord to win the Cold Tarn dispute.
divergence.consequence: The Accord gains an eastern harbour and Fearno is ringed by the crown's friends.

divergence.what: A crew, foreign or the jarl's own, kills a white spear-whale.
divergence.consequence: The east coast holds the whale-oath broken; the jarl must hang the crew's captain or lose his seat to a moot of captains, and every poor catch of the next seasons is laid at the door of whoever let it happen.

countries.name: Worlond

founding.story: The forest clans of the neck had always charged a little to let travellers through the Worlond Forest, but it was the Neck Road Compact of 4A 1214 that made a lordship of them: the crowns of Coldor and Gunwyn wanted one man to answer for the forest stages, and the clans chose Yorak Hozening of Tarvak, who built the waystations and kept them stocked with fodder and dry wood from the thaw to the first snows.

roots.story: The Worlond Forest is where the Sunfields' people parted. The clans who walked south over the neck came down from the Neridor Gap into the forest, and at the great clearing that is now Tarvak, half-way between the Gap and the West Lands, those who meant to go on and those who could walk no further made their farewells. The forest clans' tale says that each party planted a young fir at the clearing's edge, the walkers' fir on the south side and the stayers' fir on the north, and that in time the two trees grew together into one trunk, so that the forest belongs to both lands and neither may cut it. The stayers became the forest clans, who learned to live by charcoal, timber and the passing trade, and whose oldest law is the Stage Law: a traveller from either side who reaches a forest fire must be given dry wood and fodder for the night, and no forest man may take sides between the north and the south. The Neck Road Compact of 4A 1214 only gave a lord to what the clans had always done, and the Hozening lords still swear their office under the Twin Firs with one hand on the north side of the trunk and one on the south. In 4A 1748 Worlond sells timber to both, keeps the stages for both, and fears above everything a war that would make it choose between the two halves of one tree.

sign.device: The Twin Firs: two black fir trees grown together from one trunk, on a field of gold, with a green hem of fir-needles.
sign.origin: The Twin Firs stand at the edge of the clearing of Tarvak, and the forest clans hold that they are the two firs planted when the walkers and the stayers of the Sunfields parted. The clans sewed the joined trees on the cloths hung by their forest fires long before there was a lord, and Yorak Hozening took them as the sign of the Lordship of the Stages in 4A 1214, because the compact asked one man to answer to both crowns and the tree already did; the Burning of Hozoson in 4A 1390 stopped short of the clearing, which the forest folk count as the trees' own luck.
sign.meaning: One forest for both lands and a fire on the road for every traveller; to a crown that would make Worlond choose, it says that splitting the tree kills both halves.

dynasties.name: The Hozening lords of the forest stages
dynasties.notable: Descended from Yorak Hozening, the first Lord of the Stages; the lordship passes to the eldest son or daughter who has walked the whole road from the Gap to the West Lands.

events.name: The Parting at Tarvak
events.summary: The walkers of the Sunfields who went on south and the clans who stayed in the forest parted at the clearing of Tarvak, each planting a fir; the two trees grew together, and the forest clans kept the Stage Law from that day.

events.name: The Neck Road Compact
events.summary: Worlond took the forest stages of the Neck Road under the compact between Coldor and Gunwyn and became a lordship.

events.name: The Burning of Hozoson
events.summary: A summer fire took the glen of Hozoson and a third of the forest stages; Coldor and Gunwyn both sent timber-men to rebuild the road before the autumn wagons came.

events.name: The Hull-Timber Contract
events.summary: Varnondor's king bought Worlond's tallest pines for the hulls of his sea watch, and the forest's timber has gone south by the Neck Road and the Grey River ever since.

countries.capitalReason: Tarvak, the forest-place, is the largest clearing on the Neck Road, half-way between the Gap and the West Lands, where wagons must stop for a night whichever way they travel.
countries.today: About a hundred and sixty thousand foresters, charcoal-burners and waystation keepers live in the Worlond Forest on the neck. The lord keeps the stages for both crowns, sells timber to the West and hopes nobody ever fights over the road.

divergence.what: Worlond closes its forest stages to traffic from one side in a quarrel over the compact.
divergence.consequence: The Neck Road becomes a weapon: the West or the Cold Lands loses the other's goods, and travellers on the road are stranded in the forest.

divergence.what: The lord sells the whole winter's cut to the western courts for the hulls of the Crossing.
divergence.consequence: The West builds its fleet faster, Coldor's ports go short of timber, and Worlond grows rich on a war it never meant to join.

divergence.what: A crown at war fells or burns the Twin Firs at Tarvak.
divergence.consequence: The forest clans hold the Stage Law broken against that crown, refuse its travellers fire and fodder on every stage, and the Gunwyn clans of the West Lands take the felling as an insult to the walkers' kin.

countries.name: Poloto

founding.story: Aenoran ships built a trading post at the mouth of the Fandan around 1A 310, where the Cold Sea freezes latest and the river carries furs down from the interior. When Aenor's grip failed in 1A 905 the harbour men who had kept the post for Parim kept it for themselves, wrote their dues into a harbour book and chose a Harbour-Master from among the guild of pilots, and Fandhavn has been a free port under its guild ever since.

roots.story: Fandhavn's guild counts its history from two ships. The older pilots say that the Fandan mouth was where the last sea-craft of the Sunfields put out west for the isles, and that the river ice has always been read by those who stayed behind; the first ship the guild remembers by name, though, is the Aenoran post's ship that came to the Fandan mouth around 1A 310, whose pilot was a man of the Coldic coast hired at Alorio because no southerner could read the river ice. The post's pilots were his apprentices, and the guild that chose the first Harbour-Master in 1A 905 was theirs. The second ship is the one they burned. In 3A 702 servants of the Necromancer's Order moored at Fandhavn to load the dead they had bought from a starving coast clan, and Harbour-Master Zenka Grindair, with the Fandan chiefs' riders on the quay, set the ship alight and pushed it off with the first pilot's steering oar, whose blade was charred red in the burning. From that night come the harbour's laws: no ship may load the dead at Fandhavn, a ship that refuses a guild pilot is not protected, the harbour book records every ship and every refusal, and the free port sells to every flag but bows to none. The charred oar hangs over the guild's book still, and the free port of 4A 1748 is proud above all of being the harbour that the Necromancer's ship never left.

sign.device: The Burned Oar: a white steering oar standing upright with its blade red, on a deep blue field, with a white hem of river-ice blocks.
sign.origin: The first pilot's steering oar was kept by the guild as its master's staff long before 3A 702, but on the night of the March of Bones Harbour-Master Zenka Grindair used it to push the burning ship of the Necromancer's buyers away from the quay, and its blade came back charred red. The guild has carried the oar with its red blade at the head of every harbour procession since, sewn it on the flag that flies over the book-house, and had every Harbour-Master swear his office with his hand on the burned wood.
sign.meaning: A free harbour piloted by its own and closed to the trade in the dead; it promises every honest captain a guild pilot and the harbour's protection, and warns any power of the dead that the port remembers what it burned.

dynasties.name: The harbour guild of Fandhavn
dynasties.notable: Masters are chosen by the pilots' guild for life; Harbour-Master Zenka Grindair, who burned the Necromancer's ship in 3A 702 with the Fandan chiefs' help, is the guild's great name.

events.name: The Pilot of the Post
events.summary: The Aenoran trading post at the Fandan mouth hired a Coldic pilot from Alorio to read the river ice, and his apprentices became the pilots' guild that would one day keep the harbour for itself.

events.name: The Free Harbour
events.summary: The post at the Fandan mouth stopped paying Parim and became a free port under its pilots' guild.

events.name: The March of Bones
events.summary: The guild let the Fandan chiefs burn the ship of the Necromancer's buyers at its moorings, and the harbour book still records the date in red.

events.name: The Charts of the Pupor
events.summary: Fandhavn's pilots bought the new island charts and opened a regular trade to the Pupor Isles, carrying furs and ivory south for sailcloth.

countries.capitalReason: Fandhavn stands at the Fandan mouth on the Cold Sea, the harbour of the north that stays open longest each year, where the river brings the interior's goods to the sea.
countries.today: About sixty thousand people live in the free port and on the Poloto plain, under a harbour guild that sells to everyone and swears to nobody. A House of the First Light keeps the port's grain-roll and a hospital by the quay.

divergence.what: The guild opens Fandhavn to the western fleets as a supply harbour in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The Crossing gains a northern harbour that stays open late in the year, and Coldor is pressed to choose whether a free port in its valley may take sides.

divergence.what: The guild accepts the Winter Crown in return for the crown's granaries.
divergence.consequence: Coldor gains its second great harbour, and the free towns of the coast lose their last free port.

divergence.what: A ship carrying the dead, or crewed by them, seeks harbour at Fandhavn during the last war.
divergence.consequence: The guild burns it at the quay as it did in 3A 702, the free port becomes the first harbour of the north openly set against the dead, and every crown that fights them can count on Fandhavn's pilots.

countries.name: Holdon

founding.story: The south-coast clans who had kept the hunting truce with the shelf yeti since 2A 1288 grew rich on the snowline fair at Fentene, and in 4A 1120 they crowned Bran Grindair, the fair's keeper, as their king so that one hand would hold the fair's peace. Holdon's kings are still judged by one thing, which is whether the fair was good.

roots.story: Before there was a truce on the south coast there was the Red Ice. The coast clans, who came down to the Cold Ocean after the Sunfields broke and lived by the seal, and the shelf yeti, who had hunted the Yeti Shallows long before men came, fought for the seal-grounds over so many winters that the coast songs give that time no other name. Holdon's tale is that in 2A 1288 the Eldest of the shelf came down alone to the snowline at Fentene, where an old market-ground of the Sunfields lay under the moss, laid a seal-hide on the ice, pressed its open hand into seal-blood on it and waited, until the coast chiefs understood and the eldest of them pressed his own small hand into the middle of the yeti's. The truce was sung, the seal-grounds were divided and the first snowline fair was held to seal it. From the Hand-Hide come Holdon's customs: the fair-peace that no blade may break, the rule that a yeti and a man who meet on a seal-ground withdraw each to their own side, the goblins' welcome at the fair since 2A 1290, and above all the judging of every king by one thing, whether the fair was good. In 4A 1120 the clans crowned Bran Grindair, the fair's keeper, so that one hand would hold the peace, and every Grindair king since has renewed the Hand-Hide at his first fair by pressing his own hand into the old print.

sign.device: The Hand-Hide: a great white open yeti hand, palm outward, with a small black human hand pressed into its palm, on a sea-green field, with a white hem of cut seal-hide.
sign.origin: The Hand-Hide is the seal-hide on which the Eldest of the shelf and the eldest coast chief pressed their hands in seal-blood to sing the Hunting Truce of 2A 1288; it hangs in the fair-hall at Fentene, and the dark of the human hand, dried seal-blood, is renewed by each Grindair king at his first fair. The coast clans sewed the two hands on the pennant that flies over Fentene while the fair-peace holds, and when Bran Grindair was crowned in 4A 1120 the pennant became the kingdom's banner, so that Holdon's flag is the sign that the fair is open.
sign.meaning: The fair-peace between men, yeti and goblins, and a king judged by his fair; the banner raised promises that no blade is drawn at Fentene, and the banner struck means that the truce is broken.

dynasties.name: The Grindair kings of Fentene
dynasties.notable: Founded by Bran Grindair, keeper of the snowline fair; the crown passes to the eldest child, who must first keep the fair for a year as the king's deputy.

events.name: The Red Ice
events.summary: In the worst winter of the long seal-wars the coast clans and the shelf yeti killed one another on the Yeti Shallows until neither side could hunt, the memory that the Hunting Truce was sung to end.

events.name: The Hunting Truce of the Shelf
events.summary: The south-coast chiefs and the Eldest of the shelf yeti agreed which seal-grounds each would hunt, and the first snowline fair was held at Fentene to seal it.

events.name: The Crowning of the Fair-Keeper
events.summary: The coast clans crowned Bran Grindair, keeper of the snowline fair, at Fentene, so that one hand would hold the fair's peace for men, yeti and goblins alike.

events.name: The Spring Quarrel
events.summary: Holdon's herders drove their beasts to winter in Glimkit's warm valleys and the goblins drove them out again with traps; the quarrel was settled at the fair with a yearly gift of grain for grazing rights in the bitterest winters.

rivalries.nature: Trade and quarrel over the warm springs, settled at the fair each year and reopened each winter.

countries.capitalReason: Fentene sits at the snowline above the south coast, where the yeti come down from the shelf and the goblins up from their valleys, and where the fair has been held since the Hunting Truce; before Holdon was crowned it was the shelf yeti's chief meeting-place with men.
countries.today: About eighty thousand people live along the south coast facing the Coldor Channel. The king keeps the fair, the yeti come down each Long Light, the goblins bring traps and lamp-fat, and the springs quarrel simmers as it always has.

divergence.what: A raid on the snowline fair, by Holdon's own young men or by strangers, spills yeti blood.
divergence.consequence: The Hunting Truce breaks, the shelf clans close their country to men and every crown loses its only envoy route to the yeti.

divergence.what: Holdon seizes the warm springs in a bitter winter.
divergence.consequence: The coast herds survive the winter, but the goblins of Glimkit become an unruly warren inside the kingdom, and the lamps go out at the fair.

divergence.what: The Hand-Hide is burned or carried off in a raid on Fentene.
divergence.consequence: The shelf clans take the truce as unsung until a new hide is pressed, the fair cannot open, and only a king who goes alone to the snowline as the first Eldest did can begin it again.

countries.name: Glimkit

founding.story: Goblin warrens driven north by the wars of the Long Grief crossed the Coldor Channel on its winter ice around 2A 1000 and found, deep in the southern face of the Coldor Mountains, valleys where hot springs kept the snow off the ground. They dug their warrens round the largest spring and built Drikzig, the hall of the warm water, and the biggest hobgoblin among them was made chief so that the coast clans would think twice before coming to drive them out.

roots.story: The goblins of Glimkit remember the south only as the country of the burning roads. When the wars of the Long Grief drove their warrens north around 2A 1000, a column of warren-folk with a few hobgoblins and their bone-hounds reached the coast facing the Coldor Channel in the Long Dark, where goblins should never be, and the warrens tell that they would have died on the shore if a lamp-keeper called Drik had not seen, across the frozen channel, a pale plume rising from the mountains under the stars. Drik closed his lamp against the wind with panes of horn and led the column over the ice toward the plume, and his lantern was the only light they had; those who lost sight of it froze. The plume was the breath of the great spring of Agoron, and the warrens dug in around it and built Drikzig, the hall of the warm water. From the crossing come the Warren Luck and its laws: every warren keeps a closed lantern burning that was lit from Drik's, a warren whose lantern goes out is doomed until it is lit again from the hall, the hot springs are the mountain's breath and bathing in them is the one solemn rite, and no goblin goes out on open snow without a lantern-bearer. The hobgoblin chief is made big enough to frighten the coast clans, but the warrens obey the lantern-keepers, and Plickit the Broad, the chief of 4A 1748, knows that the lantern in the hall matters more than he does.

sign.device: The Crossing Lantern: a closed copper lantern with green horn panes hanging from a short black chain, on a black field, with a white hem of steam-curls.
sign.origin: The lantern is Drik's, which led the warrens over the winter ice of the Coldor Channel; it hangs in the hall of the great spring at Drikzig, and every warren's own lantern was lit from it. The goblins hammered its shape into the copper badges their trappers wore to the first snowline fair in 2A 1290, so that the coast clans would know that a goblin with a lantern came to trade and not to steal, and the same shape, sewn in green and copper on black, has flown over Drikzig ever since.
sign.meaning: The Warren Luck: while the lantern burns the warren lives; it promises good traps and lamps at the fair and warns that the warrens will defend to the last the springs that saved them.

dynasties.name: The hobgoblin chiefs of Drikzig
dynasties.notable: Each chief is the biggest hobgoblin the warrens can agree on and rules this valley and no other; the warrens obey their cleverest goblins, and the chief obeys the warrens more often than he admits. The present chief is called Plickit the Broad.

events.name: The Crossing of the Ice
events.summary: The goblins crossed the Coldor Channel on the winter ice and settled round the hot springs.

events.name: The First Fair
events.summary: Goblin trappers came up to the new snowline fair at Fentene with lamps and traps, and the coast clans who had fought them began to buy from them instead.

events.name: The Lantern Winter
events.summary: A coughing sickness put out the lanterns of the warrens of Belor one by one until the last lantern-keeper carried a coal up to Drikzig and relit them from Drik's lantern; Belor has paid the hall a lamp-tithe ever since.

events.name: The Spring Quarrel
events.summary: Holdon's herds were driven out of the warm valleys with traps, and the quarrel was settled at the fair with grain for grazing rights in the bitterest winters.

rivalries.nature: The springs: trade in summer, traps in winter.

countries.capitalReason: Drikzig is built round the largest hot spring of the Coldor Mountains, which the goblins call the mountain's breath and bathe in as their one solemn rite; without the spring there would be no goblins in the north at all.
countries.today: About fifteen thousand goblins and a few hobgoblins live in the steaming valleys of Agoron and Belor, making the best traps and lamps of the north and riding shaggy bone-hounds in summer. They join no league and leave their valleys only for the fair, and Coldor's crown has never tried to tax them.

divergence.what: The warrens open their valleys to a crown that swears to guard the springs.
divergence.consequence: That crown gains goblin traps and lamps for its forts, and the goblins gain a protector they will expect to keep its word.

divergence.what: Glimkit sells its lamps and traps to Melkgard's forts.
divergence.consequence: The March Forts grow harder to take by night, and Holdon, which trades with the goblins, finds itself between the warrens and the crown.

divergence.what: Drik's lantern in the hall at Drikzig goes out, by mischance, sabotage or a conqueror's hand.
divergence.consequence: Every warren holds itself doomed, the trappers stay home from the fair and the warrens may abandon their valleys unless a lantern lit from Drik's can be found in some warren's keeping and carried back to the hall.

countries.name: Xison

founding.story: The upland clans between Fandanar and the west coast had suffered in the Forty Winters' Quarrel when both crowns' riders used the high road, and in 4A 902 the chiefs of Xison, Rion and Yeneldmore met at Akahew and swore a road league: each clan keeps its stretch of the road, all share the tolls, and no army crosses the uplands without the moot's leave.

roots.story: The uplands between Fandanar and the west coast were the amber road of the Sunfields, by which the amber of the western shore went inland to the old halls, and the upland clans descend from the carriers who kept its waystations and stayed on the high moors when the halls emptied. For two ages they were nobody's: there were no crowns to be anybody's, and the road carried reindeer hides, amber and the occasional Aenoran trader. The Forty Winters' Quarrel changed that. Both crowns' riders used the high road to raid each other, and in one Long Dark late in the quarrel the clans of Xison, Rion and Yeneldmore saw their waystations burned by both sides. At Akahew in 4A 902 the three chiefs did what the carriers' songs said the old road-keepers had done against bandits: they had their smiths forge a chain from the broken stirrups and bridle-iron of the riders who had died on their road, three great links for the three clans, and stretched it across the road on two posts, and no army may pass it without the road-moot's leave. From the chain come the league's laws: each clan keeps its own stretch of the road, the tolls are shared, the chain is lifted only by the moot's speaker, and a crown's wagon pays like any carter's. The lower toll that the crown won in 4A 1360 is still resented, and in 4A 1748 the league leans to Coldor since the White Year but keeps its chain on the posts.

sign.device: The Akahew Chain: three great black chain-links joined in a row across the field, on red, with a gold hem of amber beads.
sign.origin: The device is the chain the three upland clans forged at Akahew in 4A 902 from the stirrup-iron and bridle-iron of the riders of both crowns who had died raiding on the high road, one link each for Xison, Rion and Yeneldmore. It still hangs across the road on its two posts at Akahew and is lifted only by the speaker of the road-moot; the league sewed it on its toll-pennants the year it was forged, so that every carter on the high road would know where the moot's law began, while the speakers' seal keeps the Esroming reindeer.
sign.meaning: A road held in common by three clans and closed to every army without the moot's leave; to a crown it says that the uplands pay the toll and take the toll, and will be nobody's road to war.

dynasties.name: The moot-speakers of Akahew
dynasties.notable: The road-moot chooses a speaker for three Long Lights at a time; the Esroming hearth of the Rion moors has given the most, and the league's seal shows their reindeer.

events.name: The Amber Road
events.summary: The carriers of the Sunfields kept waystations on the high moors between the western shore and the old halls, bringing amber inland, and stayed on the moors as clans when the halls emptied.

events.name: The Burning of the Stations
events.summary: In one Long Dark of the Forty Winters' Quarrel the riders of both crowns burned the upland waystations of Xison, Rion and Yeneldmore, which drove the three clans to the road league seven years later.

events.name: The Road League
events.summary: The upland clans swore the road league at Akahew after the Forty Winters' Quarrel.

events.name: The Toll of the Uplands
events.summary: Coldor demanded that crown wagons go free on the high road; the moot refused, the crown sent its grain to Alorio by sea for three years, and the matter ended in a lower toll rather than none.

events.name: The Founding of Norrak
events.summary: The Rion herders built the moor town of Norrak on the upland road so that the reindeer markets need not go down to the coast.

events.name: The White Year
events.summary: Coldor's granaries fed the upland clans, and the road-moot let the crown's wagons pass free for that winter alone.

countries.capitalReason: Akahew is the market town where the upland road meets the coast road above Alorio, the natural place for a league whose whole wealth is the traffic between the crown and its western port.
countries.today: About a hundred and twenty thousand upland clansfolk keep the high road, trade amber and reindeer hides and grumble at every crown wagon that pays the lower toll. The moot leans to Coldor since the White Year but keeps its gate.

divergence.what: The road-moot gives the high road to the Winter Crown in return for a seat at the Frost Moot.
divergence.consequence: Coldor's capital and western port are joined under one law, and the uplands lose the tolls that made them free.

divergence.what: The moot closes the high road to all armies in the last war.
divergence.consequence: Coldor's ports can only be reached by sea in winter, and any crown at war in the north must go round the uplands or through them.

divergence.what: A crown's army cuts the chain at Akahew instead of asking the moot to lift it.
divergence.consequence: The road league turns against that crown to a man, the high road becomes a country of ambushes for its wagons, and the other crown is offered the road at the old toll.

countries.name: Pertolor

founding.story: The shepherds of the sheep vale east of the Ormolak country, the only valley of the north where sheep do better than reindeer, built a hall at Minsentia in 4A 760 and gave their best breeder, Hildra Hozening, the keeping of the vale's wool-market. The vale has been courted by both crowns since they were crowns, because its wool and mutton feed whoever holds its friendship.

roots.story: The sheep vale east of the Ormolak country is the only valley of the north where sheep do better than reindeer, and its people say they know why. In their tale, long before the vale had a hall, a shepherd clan of the Sunfields lost its flock in a whiteout on the high ground and gave it up for dead, and in the thaw the flock came down out of the valley of Mp'E behind a black-faced ram, fat and whole, with no one to say where it had wintered. The clan settled where the ram stopped and has bred from his line ever since, and the vale has paid what it calls the ram's due: each Long Light the shepherds carry a loaf and a fleece to the start of the Silent Road beyond the town of Yeldenne and leave them for the hall, and nobody walks on. The vale's customs come from that debt: a shepherd who loses a beast in the snow does not curse the high ground, nobody of the vale goes up the Silent Road, the black-faced rams are never sold out of the vale, and the town of Yeldenne below the silent castle, which lies in the vale's land, has always been treated as kin and never taxed as a subject. The Hozening lords, who were given the wool-market in 4A 760, keep the ram's due along with the market, and the vale's careful friendship with both crowns in 4A 1748 is the same habit seen from below: the vale keeps faith with whatever feeds it and asks no questions of the high ground.

sign.device: The Black-Faced Ram: a white ram with a black face and black curled horns, standing, on a deep green field, with a red hem of woven wool.
sign.origin: The ram is the leader of the flock that came down out of the valley of Mp'E in the thaw, from whose line every black-faced ram of the vale is bred. The shepherds stitched him on the cloth in which the ram's due is carried to the Silent Road long before the vale had a lord, and Hildra Hozening hung that cloth over the wool-market at Minsentia when she built the hall in 4A 760; the lords have flown it since and have refused every offer to quarter it with the arms of either crown, even after the Vale Marriage of 4A 1590.
sign.meaning: Faith kept with whatever feeds the vale, a flock that comes home and a debt to the high ground that is paid and never questioned; to the crowns it says that the vale will feed a friend and has not yet chosen one.

dynasties.name: The Hozening lords of the sheep vale
dynasties.notable: Descended from Hildra Hozening; the lordship passes to the eldest child, and the family marries into both crowns' houses when it can.

dynasties.name: The headmen of Simoto, Sten Ezhson's line
dynasties.notable: The valley chooses its headman from the founder's kin; he keeps the bread-custom and the valley's peace with both crowns. Above the town, the lord of the hall, whom the valley names Horos, has never been seen to come down.

events.name: The Flock out of the Whiteout
events.summary: A shepherd clan of the Sunfields lost its flock in a whiteout on the high ground, and in the thaw the flock came down out of the valley of Mp'E behind a black-faced ram; the clan settled where he stopped and began to pay the ram's due.

events.name: The Hall at Minsentia
events.summary: Hildra Hozening was given the vale's wool-market and built the hall at Minsentia.

events.name: The Vale Marriage
events.summary: Lady Zena Hozening married Prince Branak of House Vording, and Coldor's queens have since counted the vale's lords as cousins; Melkgard answered by taking two Hozening sons into its oath-companies.

events.name: The White Year
events.summary: Both crowns sent grain to the vale, and the lord took both and thanked both.

events.name: The First Loaf
events.summary: Sten Ezhson laid the first loaf at the start of the Silent Road, and the valley has never let a Long Dark pass without one.

events.name: The Warlord's Climb
events.summary: A warlord of Melkgard who meant to tax the valley sent twenty oath-men up the Silent Road; none came back down, and since then neither Melkgard nor Coldor has asked Mp'E for anything.

events.name: The Southern Pilgrims
events.summary: A party of southern scholars and temple folk reached Simoto asking about a castle in the ice; the headman fed them, refused them a guide and sent them home by the Ormolak Pass.

countries.capitalReason: Minsentia stands at the head of the sheep vale where the drove roads to Faaennar and the Ormolak country meet, the market-place of the vale's wool.
countries.today: About ninety thousand herders live in the sheep vale and on the Faaennar plain. The lord is cousin to the Winter Queen and godfather to a Melkgard captain, and he intends to stay both for as long as the crowns let him. The valley of Mp'E above the Ormolak Pass, with the town of Simoto and the castle above it, lies in the lordship's land; the headman keeps the loaf on the Silent Road every Long Dark.

divergence.what: The lord chooses a side in the Cold Rivalry, by marriage or by oath.
divergence.consequence: The wool and mutton of the vale go to one crown alone, and the other treats the vale as an enemy's larder.

divergence.what: Coldor or Melkgard takes the vale by force.
divergence.consequence: The taker gains the vale's herds and loses every border clan's trust, and the Cold Rivalry becomes open war.

divergence.what: The ram's due goes unpaid for a Long Light, because of war in the vale or a lord who scorns the custom.
divergence.consequence: The shepherds fear for their flocks and the lord's hold on the vale weakens, the town of Simoto shuts its doors to the vale's men, and nobody in the vale can say what the high ground will do, which is worse than any answer.

divergence.what: The headman calls the valley's men to guard the empty road to the hall when strangers come asking.
divergence.consequence: The hall's defenders are mortal men with bows, few but forewarned, and a party that tries to force the road meets them first.

divergence.what: A hungry winter makes the valley eat the loaf it owes the Silent Road.
divergence.consequence: The valley's belief says the Watcher will wake; what happens in the hall is not known, but the town would never be the same in its own eyes.

countries.name: Omar

founding.story: The Omar clan came onto the border moor between the Ormolak country and the valley of Mp'E in 2A 1520, driving their reindeer ahead of a hard winter, and built the hill-fort of Vaesdeon on the one rise that commands the moor. They have held it since by being too poor to be worth a war and too stubborn to give an oath.

roots.story: The Omar clan carries the oldest refusal in the north. Its songs say that in the last winters of the Sunfields, when the old king's stewards rode the moors demanding the clans' herds for the hall, the Omar forebears slaughtered one reindeer bull, ate it at their own fire and sent the stewards back with its skull and antlers bound to a sledge, which meant, then as now, that the clan had eaten its own and owed nothing. The clan wandered the moors for ages afterwards with that refusal as its only law, owing no oath, giving no hostage and paying debts only in kind, until Kerdok drove its herds onto the border moor between the Ormolak country and the valley of Mp'E ahead of the hard winter of 2A 1520 and built Vaesdeon on the moor's one rise. Kerdok's line keeps the clan's two laws: a chief must have spent a winter alone on the moor, as the forebears did when the king's hall fell, and every debt is counted on the antler-tally that hangs in the hill-fort, a notch cut for each gift taken and a notch filled for each repaid. The skull went to Melkgard's warlord in 4A 1150 for the same reason it went to the old king's stewards, and in 4A 1748 the tally shows a debt to Coldor for the Hill-Fort Winter and one to Melkgard for the White Year, which the chief counts with great care and pays to neither.

sign.device: The Refusal Skull: a white reindeer skull with full antlers, facing outward, on a black field, with a white hem of notches like a tally.
sign.origin: The skull is the clan's old sign of refusal, first sent bound to a sledge to the stewards of the old king of the Sunfields and sent again to Melkgard's warlord in 4A 1150 when he demanded the clan's oath. A skull with its antlers hangs over the gate of Vaesdeon, and the clan painted it on the shields of the men who held the hill-fort through the siege of 4A 1412; after that siege the white skull on black became the clan's banner, and the notched hem copies the antler-tally of its debts.
sign.meaning: We have eaten our own and owe nothing: no oath, no hostage and every debt counted; to a crown that asks for an oath it is the answer before the question is asked.

dynasties.name: Kerdok's line
dynasties.notable: The clan moot chooses its chief from the descendants of Kerdok, who built the hill-fort; the chief must have spent a winter alone on the moor.

events.name: The Skull to the Stewards
events.summary: When the old king's stewards demanded the clans' herds for the hall, the Omar forebears ate one bull at their own fire and sent back its skull and antlers on a sledge, the clan's sign of refusal ever since.

events.name: The Hill-Fort
events.summary: Kerdok's clan drove its herds onto the border moor ahead of a hard winter and built the hill-fort of Vaesdeon on its only rise.

events.name: The Oath Refused
events.summary: Melkgard's warlord demanded the clan's oath; the chief sent back a reindeer skull, the clan's old sign of refusal.

events.name: The Hill-Fort Winter
events.summary: Melkgard's oath-companies besieged Vaesdeon through a Long Dark until a relief of Coldic riders came over the Fandan ice; Omar has owed Coldor ever since and has never quite forgiven it the debt.

events.name: The Gifts of the White Year
events.summary: Melkgard sent salt meat and iron tools to the starving clan, and the chief took them.

rivalries.nature: The march that presses the clan hardest, with gifts and oath-demands.

countries.capitalReason: Vaesdeon stands on the only rise of the border moor, from which a watcher can see riders coming from the Ormolak country or the Fandan a day before they arrive.
countries.today: About fifty thousand herders hold the border moor, owing Coldor for the Hill-Fort Winter and Melkgard for the White Year. Their chief counts the debts and pays neither.

divergence.what: The chief swears to Melkgard.
divergence.consequence: The march reaches the road to Mp'E, and Coldor loses its nearest friend on the warlord's border.

divergence.what: The clan guides southern strangers across the moor to the valley of Mp'E for silver.
divergence.consequence: Strangers reach the silent castle without passing Melkgard's forts, and the valley folk count Omar among those who sold the road.

divergence.what: A crown pays the clan's debts to the other crown and asks for the tally in return.
divergence.consequence: The chief must either fill the last notches and owe that crown alone, which ends the clan's oldest freedom, or send back the skull a third time and make an enemy of the richer crown.

countries.name: Portogalor

founding.story: The last fleet of north-coast raiders broke on Melkgard's forts in 3A 410, and its survivors, who could not go home and could not stay, settled the bare coast below the Olsuaon Massif and turned from raiding to sealing. Their captain, Ulvar Azlak, built the sealers' harbour at Fellodor, and his descendants have kept it as lords of the coast.

roots.story: The sealers of Fellodor are proud of being descended from the enemy. Their forebears were the sea-raiders of the Frozen Ocean coast who burned the Ormolak valley for ages, a people whose songs begin at sea and say nothing of where the first ships were launched, only that something behind them in the far north was worse than any wind; a belief of Fandanar's fire-keepers holds that they fled the country of the dead, and the sealers neither confirm nor deny it. When the last great fleet broke on the forts of the Gulf of Minnolomak in 3A 410, its captain Ulvar Azlak took the survivors along the bare coast below the Olsuaon Massif, dragged the last whole hulls up the beach and turned them keel-up to make halls, so that no man of the fleet could put to sea and go back to whatever they had fled. From the upturned hulls come the customs of the north coast: a lord's hall is always roofed with a ship's keel, the sealers bury a worn-out hull and never burn one, a new captain spends his first night under the keel of the first hall, and raiding is remembered with pride and forbidden by law. In 4A 1748 Fellodor sells hides, ivory and seal-fat along the Frozen Sea, its captains wear the bear-mantles of the Bear Winter, and its lords are careful not to remind Melkgard whose sons they are.

sign.device: The Keel-Hall: a black ship's hull turned keel-up, with a row of red oar-ports along its side, on a white field, with a grey hem of sea-ice.
sign.origin: Ulvar Azlak's men dragged the last whole hulls of the broken fleet up the beach at Fellodor in 3A 410 and turned them keel-up as halls so that nobody could sail back, and the first of them still roofs the lord's hall. The survivors painted it in pitch on the sealskin they raised over the beach to tell Melkgard's watchers that the raiders had come to stay, and the sealers have flown the black keel on white ever since; the red oar-ports are the oars they burned that first night for warmth, the only wood of the fleet they ever burned.
sign.meaning: A people who came to burn and stayed to build: a promise that the north coast will never raid again, and a reminder that it remembers how.

dynasties.name: The Azlak lords of Fellodor
dynasties.notable: Descended from the raider-captain Ulvar Azlak; the lord is chosen from the family by the sealing captains.

events.name: The Raiders Broken
events.summary: Ulvar Azlak's fleet broke on the forts of the Gulf of Minnolomak and its survivors settled the north coast.

events.name: The Keel-Halls
events.summary: Ulvar Azlak's survivors dragged their last hulls up the beach below the Olsuaon Massif and turned them keel-up as halls, so that no man of the broken fleet could sail home again.

events.name: The Frozen Sea Trade
events.summary: Fellodor's sealers opened a summer trade along the Frozen Sea coast to Minnolomak and Fandhavn, selling hides and ivory for grain.

events.name: The Bear Winter
events.summary: Great white bears came ashore in numbers after a poor seal year and killed sealers on the ice; the lord's bear-hunt that spring made a chief's mantle for every captain who joined it.

rivalries.nature: Old enemies who became trading partners; the march still calls the sealers raiders when it wants their harbour.

countries.capitalReason: Fellodor is the one harbour of the bare north coast that the Olsuaon Massif shelters from the north wind, close to the sealing grounds of Pandar.
countries.today: About fifty thousand sealers live on the north coast and the massif, selling hides, ivory and seal-fat on the Frozen Sea trade. They are proud of their raider forebears and careful not to remind Melkgard of them.

divergence.what: The lord sends his sealing fleet to watch the far northern waters in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The north coast gains a watch on the cold sea, and any landing there is seen from the ice.

divergence.what: Melkgard takes Fellodor as a second harbour.
divergence.consequence: The march gains the north coast and the sealers' hulls, and its quarrel with Coldor reaches the sea.

divergence.what: A lord of Fellodor relaunches the first keel-hall to lead his sealers to war.
divergence.consequence: The north coast takes it as the end of the raiders' oath; the sealers fight hard and well, but Melkgard and every coast clan remember whose sons they are, and Fellodor's harbour is closed to them for a generation after the war.

countries.name: Kvittumm

founding.story: The reindeer clans of the far north-west, who move with their herds between the giants' foothills and the Orewell lowland, first met as one confederacy in 2A 1312, when the Frost-King of the heights would treat with no more than one voice. They swore the toll-peace at Xitore together, and the white-hills confederacy has met each Long Dark since at its winter moot-place of Esrom.

roots.story: The reindeer clans of the far north-west say that when the Sunfields' fields failed their forebears did not follow the walkers south or the sailors west but followed the herds, which went north-west into the ice country where no field had ever been, and learned from the reindeer how to live in it. The clans' first law is the herd's: the herd moves and the people move with it, no clan fences grazing, and a clan that loses its herd is taken in by the others until it has calves again.
